## Guide to the supplementary material

Appendix A presents the literature review that supports the study.
Appendix B describes the use and verification of AI-assisted research.
Appendix C connects the mathematical formulation to its software implementations
and explains how solutions are validated. Appendix D describes the data,
effective parameter values and preparation of the experimental instances.
Readers reproducing the calculations can begin with D and then follow C.

The [bibliography](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/model-agrologistic/blob/1b54023f4e0c0c27aba64883b1e9cf25817ad0f8/manuscript/references.bib) and
[review-method references](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/model-agrologistic/blob/1b54023f4e0c0c27aba64883b1e9cf25817ad0f8/manuscript/review-methods.bib)
provide the sources cited throughout the supplement. Links to software and
data records identify fixed versions; each computational result is associated
with the version and input used in its experiment.

# Appendix B Human-supervised AI-assisted research

## B1 Purpose and scope

AI assistants supported mathematical discussion, software development and
scientific writing. Human researchers defined the research question, selected
the assumptions, evaluated proposed changes and interpreted the results.
The mathematical foundation is attributed to @rosa2026thesis. AI assistance
is described here to make the research procedure transparent; it is not
evidence of an independent origin for the model or a measured productivity gain.

Three types of evidence serve different purposes. A discussion identifies a
proposal. Versioned code and tests establish what was implemented and examined.
An experiment record identifies the calculation performed and its numerical
outcome. A proposal becomes part of the method only after mathematical review,
implementation and verification appropriate to its scientific role.

## B2 Tools and human responsibilities

Gurobot supported early formulation discussions. Gemini and GPT systems
assisted with technical criticism and alternative interpretations. ChatGPT
supported coordination and writing, while Codex assisted with implementation,
tests, diagnostics and documentation. Available records identify these roles
without establishing a complete chronology of model versions or the authorship
of every code fragment.

These generative assistants are distinct from the numerical tools. Python
organizes data and calculations; Gurobi and SCIP solve mathematical programs;
Pyomo expresses a solver-independent formulation, with HiGHS and CBC interfaces.
GitHub maintains the software history, and Slurm schedules the HPC experiments.
Researchers executed the experimental commands and evaluated the returned
evidence. A completed software process was not treated as proof of a feasible
or sufficiently accurate solution.

## B3 Mathematical review before implementation

Review began with the connection between the planning problem and its
equations. The researchers checked which decisions preceded uncertainty,
which decisions varied by scenario, and which quantities represented stock,
throughput, investment or constraint exceedance. They also examined indexing,
units, eligibility and objective coefficients.

This review was especially important for the two-stage implementation.
Investment must be shared across scenarios and charged once, while operating
costs are probability weighted. Scenario probabilities do not scale the
physical balances. Similarly, static storage and daily handling rates cannot
be interchanged merely because both appear in capacity constraints.
AI-generated proposals were assessed against these requirements before adoption.

Exploratory discussions also considered alternative objectives, GAMS
representations and decomposition. These discussions did not constitute
additional experiments in the extensive-form cohort reported in the article.
Only the implemented, tested formulation and its original computational
outputs support that cohort.

## B4 Numerical verification

The procedure in Figure B.1 connects human review, implementation, small
verification examples and large experiments. Return arrows indicate revision
when a discrepancy is found.

![Figure B.1. Human-supervised research and verification. Mathematical review precedes implementation; analytical examples, software tests and original experiment outputs support interpretation.](../figures/human_ai_workflow.png)

Small examples tested objective reconstruction, investment charged once,
probability weighting, deterministic specialization, capacity units and
activation conditions. The returned large-instance decisions were then checked
in original units against material balances, eligibility and capacity
relationships. All fourteen objective components were reconstructed separately.

These checks are complementary. Agreement of objective values can conceal a
constraint violation, and an aggregate material balance can conceal a local
violation. A small optimization gap bounds uncertainty about the penalized
objective; it does not establish adequate service or accurate financial costs
when artificial penalties dominate the total.

## B5 Traceability of a computational result

For each experiment, the retained record identifies the source version,
input workbook, facility population, scenario design, solver settings,
resource limits, decisions and validation outcome. This association permits
another researcher to connect a numerical table to the calculation that
produced it. Partial and failed attempts are retained alongside successful
ones to avoid selective reporting.

The [mathematical contract](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/model-agrologistic/blob/1b54023f4e0c0c27aba64883b1e9cf25817ad0f8/docs/mvp2_scalar_contract.md),
[implementation](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/model-agrologistic/blob/1b54023f4e0c0c27aba64883b1e9cf25817ad0f8/src/logic/optimization_gurobipy_stochastic.py) and
[independent validator](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/model-agrologistic/blob/1b54023f4e0c0c27aba64883b1e9cf25817ad0f8/src/logic/solution_validation.py)
provide a concrete route from assumptions to checked decisions. For example,
the [h500 experiment record](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/model-agrologistic/blob/1b54023f4e0c0c27aba64883b1e9cf25817ad0f8/docs/evidence/scalar_h500_2220382_review.json)
connects its input and source identities to the objective, bound, original
validation and resource observations. Appendices C and D explain the
corresponding implementation and data.

An integrity replay checks consistency of retained records and their hashes.
It does not rerun the optimizer or recompute residuals against unavailable
inputs. A fresh numerical reproduction must generate new decisions and apply
the independent validation procedure to them.

## B6 Limitations

The conversational record is incomplete. Different assistants may repeat a
common error, so agreement between them is not independent scientific review.
Tests verify specified properties and examples; they do not establish general
correctness or substitute for substantive modeling judgment. Restricted inputs
can also limit independent reconstruction of a large experiment.

The study has no controlled comparison for measuring time saved, productivity
or error reductions caused by AI assistance. Its methodological contribution
is the inspectable connection between proposals, human decisions,
implementations and numerical evidence. The authors retain responsibility for
all assumptions, reported results and conclusions.
